about: The geometry kernel's quality ledger (kernel architecture 28.8). survivors: every mutant cargo-mutants makes that the kernel's tests do not catch and the kernel keeps, keyed by file, cargo-mutants' description and the trimmed text of the mutated line, with why; in the foundation set only equivalent mutants (no input through the crate's public interface can tell them from the original) may be kept. coverage_off: every coverage(off) mark in a kernel crate, with the Kani or Verus proof that the code it hides cannot run. awaiting_proof: every foundation line the tests do not run yet, by its file, its trimmed text and how many missed lines have it, with the piece that proves it unreachable or tests it (the coverage gate landed before those proofs: owner decision of 2026-10-27); the list can only shrink. geom-test's kernel-quality binary checks both in .github/workflows/kernel-quality.yml; geom_test::quality_ledger documents the format.

survivors.reason: The two comparisons differ from their mutants only at zero. fa is not zero here: zero returned already when f(a) is zero. fb is not zero wherever its comparison is evaluated: the left operand of && is fb != 0.0. So both forms give the same sign test for every input.

At fb = 0 the whole test is false either way, by its right operand. fc is never zero: it is set only from f(a) at the start (not zero, or zero returned already), from fa (the previous fb, and a zero fb ends the search before it can become fa), or from fb in the swap, which happens only when |fc| < |fb|, so that fb is not zero. Where neither is zero, x > 0 and x >= 0 agree.

The branches differ only when |d| = tol1, and then they add the same double. d is either the bisection step xm, or an accepted interpolation p/q with p >= 0, accepted only when 2p < 3*xm*q - |tol1*q|, which needs xm*q > 0: either way d has the sign of xm (or is a zero of that sign, p/q with p = +0). So |d| = tol1 makes d equal to with_sign(tol1, xm), bit for bit, the zero cases included.

A tie |fa| = |fb| makes both refuse the interpolation and bisect. With a != c (inverse quadratic) a and b lie on the same side of c, so fa = fb, s = 1, q = 0 and 2p < 0 is false. With a == c (secant) a tie can come only from a reset or the first step, as a swap leaves |fb| < |fa|; there e = b - a and 2xm = a - b, rounded alike, so fa = fb gives q = 0 and fa = -fb gives p = |e| = |0.5*e*q|, and p < |0.5*e*q| is false.

The two differ only when q is zero, of either sign, where the mutant negates p. Then 0.5*q*previous is zero, so |p| < |0.5*q*previous| is false whatever p's sign, the vertex is refused either way, and p is used nowhere else.

survivors.line_text: let goal = if tol > rel * value.get().abs() {
survivors.reason: The goal is the larger of tol and rel*|value|. The mutant picks tol also when the two are equal, which is the same double, so the goal, and every result, is the same.

abs is private, and every caller uses what it returns only in a comparison: fast_two_sum compares abs(b) > abs(a), split compares abs(a) < 2^996, two_prod compares abs(p), abs(a) and abs(b) with powers of two. The mutant changes the result only for x = +0 or -0, where it returns the other zero, and -0 and +0 compare equal in every comparison, so no public function's result changes.

x.to_bits() & !EXPONENT_BITS clears every exponent bit, and ONE_BITS, the bits of 1.0, has only exponent bits set (field 1023, no sign, no fraction). Two words with no set bit in common give the same word under OR and XOR, so unit_binade returns the same double for every x.

survivors.line_text: let (larger, smaller) = if abs(b) > abs(a) { (b, a) } else { (a, b) };
survivors.reason: The mutant also swaps the operands when |a| = |b|. Dekker's step needs only |larger| >= |smaller|, which both orders meet, and IEEE addition is commutative, so s is the same. When a = b the two orders are the same pair; when a = -b, s is +0 and the error smaller + larger is +0 either way; for -0 and +0 the error is -0 or +0, which zero_to_plus makes +0; two infinities of one sign give (s, -s) with s infinite either way, and of opposite signs the invalid sum, a NaN whose bits Rust does not fix (the function documents NaN only as NaN). A NaN input makes both comparisons false, so neither version swaps. Every result is the same.

survivors.line_text: if y < x { y } else { x }
survivors.reason: min2 is private, and its only callers (Interval::mul, div and mul_add) pass what it returns straight to widened(). The mutant answers differently only when x and y are equal: two equal non-zero doubles have the same bits, so either is the same answer; for -0 and +0 it returns the other zero, but widened() takes next_down of the bound, which is -2^-1074 for either zero. Every interval a public operation returns has the same bits.

survivors.line_text: if y > x { y } else { x }
survivors.reason: max2 is private. In Interval::mul, div and mul_add its result goes straight to widened(), which takes next_up of the bound: +2^-1074 for either zero, so returning the other of two equal values (the only change, when x equals y) gives the same bits. Its one other caller, Interval::square's branch for an interval holding zero, passes -lo and hi with lo < 0 < hi, two positive doubles, which are equal only with the same bits.

In this branch (hi <= 0) near and far are used only as near * near, far * far and near == 0.0. IEEE 754 multiplication gives (-a) * (-a) and a * a the same bits (the product of two equal signs is positive, with the same magnitude), and -0.0 == 0.0 is true, so dropping either minus changes no bound that Interval::square, Interval::norm or anything built on them returns.

lo is the literal 0.0 (when the interval holds zero) or zero_to_plus of a rounded square moved down one step, so it is never -0. The mutant differs only when lo equals zero, and then returns the literal 0.0 where the original returns lo, which is +0 too: the same bits in every interval Interval::square returns.

sqrt_nonneg is private and its only caller, Interval::norm, passes it a sum of squares (an empty list returns [0, 0] before reaching it). Interval::square's upper bound is next_up of a non-negative double, at least 2^-1074, and Interval::add's is next_up of a sum of such bounds, so the upper bound reaching sqrt_nonneg is always positive: hi < 0 and hi == 0 are both false for every call, and the mutant changes no result of Interval::norm.

survivors.line_text: let lo = if self.lo < 0.0 { 0.0 } else { self.lo };
survivors.reason: The mutant differs only when the lower bound equals zero, and then passes the literal 0.0 on to Interval::sqrt where the original passes self.lo. Every Interval stores a zero bound as +0 (its invariant: Interval::new, widened() and square apply zero_to_plus or write 0.0), so both are +0 and Interval::norm returns the same bits.

The validity check only skips masks whose matrix has a zero determinant, so weakening it changes no result. A mask that picks two entries of one column sets two rows to the same unit vector, a zero determinant. A mask that picks two entries of one row builds the matrix of a smaller mask (the row keeps one unit vector), which the walk visited earlier and found zero, or which itself repeats a column. Checked by simulating the walk with and without the check on 4,000 random orient2d and incircle ties: every sign agreed.

survivors.line_text: let ([nx, ny, nz], [xx, xy, xz]) = (*n, x);
survivors.reason: classify runs only in side_of_tpi_hand, which Plane::side_of_tpi calls only when the generated tpi_side path returns None. That path checks its rounded inputs against their certified widths on entry, and every plane a user can make comes from Plane::through on grid points, whose coefficients lie inside those widths (G29's budget); inside them its steps cannot overflow (the certificate; G39's Verus twin of tpi_side). So no public input reaches classify, and returning None from it changes no result a user can see.

The mutant also runs the narrowing check when M equals L, a resize to the same width. Then no limb is dropped (skipping M limbs of an L-limb array leaves none, so all() holds) and the copy r has the very limbs of self, so its sign is self's: the check never returns None, and Wide::resize returns the same Some(r) for every value and every pair of widths.

i is unsigned, so `i >= 0` always holds: once i reaches 0 the loop wraps it to usize::MAX and walks down for ever, both limbs reading 0 past the array (get returns None), so the tests stop it by their timeout. It hangs; it never returns a wrong order.
The line runs only inside `if high_a != high_b`, where the two limbs differ, and for different values `<` and `<=` give the same answer, so no input can tell the mutant from the original.

The line runs only for a limb at index L or above. The crate reaches from_magnitude only through product_i128 (checked_mul_i128 has no caller outside the tests), always with four limbs and only at widths 4 and 5: crossing.rs's side::<4> and side::<5>, plane.rs's I256 products and lpi_classify::<4> and ::<5>, and the generated I256 paths. So every index is below L, the line never runs, and no input through the public interface can tell the mutant from the original. The unit tests run it at widths 2 and 3, and the Verus twin (verus/wide.rs) proves from_magnitude right at every width.

The line runs only when the magnitude's top bit is set, so the magnitude is at least 2^(64L-1). The crate reaches from_magnitude only through product_i128 (checked_mul_i128 has no caller outside the tests), always with four limbs and only at widths 4 and 5: crossing.rs's side::<4> and side::<5>, plane.rs's I256 products and lpi_classify::<4> and ::<5>, and the generated I256 paths. There the magnitude |a b| is at most 2^254, below 2^255 <= 2^(64L-1), so the line never runs and no input through the public interface can tell the mutant from the original. The unit tests run it, and the Verus twin proves from_magnitude right at every width.

For a negative v the mutant takes the other arm, `v as u128`, which reads v's two's complement as unsigned, v + 2^128: the same u the original builds as (v - i128::MIN) + 2^127 (it only avoids a cast clippy flags as losing the sign). For v = 0 the mutant takes the first arm, where 0 - i128::MIN overflows, so checked_sub gives None and u = 0, as `0 as u128` does. Every v gives the same u, so the same limbs.
The two differ only at v = 0, where the mutant takes the first arm: 0 - i128::MIN = 2^127 overflows i128, so checked_sub gives None and u = 0, the same u as the original's `0 as u128`.
This arm runs for a negative v, where d = v - i128::MIN lies in 0..2^127, so bit 127 of d is clear: setting it with | and flipping it with ^ both give d + 2^127.

The line is the arm for a contribution at limb L, past the result's limbs: it returns None on overflow. checked_mul_i128 is pub(crate), and its only callers are the generated exact paths (tpi_side, tpi_weight and the like), which check their inputs against the certified widths on entry; inside those widths every product fits its limbs (the certificate; G39's Verus twin proves checked_mul_i128 exact), so prod and carry are both 0 whenever this arm runs, and || and && give the same answer for every public input.

survivors.line_text: let shared = if M < L { M } else { L };
survivors.reason: The mutant makes shared L when M < L (and when M == L, where L is M anyway); widening is unchanged (shared is L either way). Narrowing then runs the copy loop over L indices instead of M: the extra ones, M to L − 1, read limbs of self but find no slot in out (get_mut returns None for i >= M), so they write nothing, and out is the same array. Every value resizes to the same result.

survivors.line_text: let shared = if M < L { M } else { L };
survivors.reason: The two comparisons differ only when M equals L, and then both branches give the same number (M is L), so shared, the copy and the result are the same for every value and every pair of widths.

The mutant also tests the sign when M equals L, a resize to the same width. Then r has the very limbs of self, so its sign is self's and the test is false: resize returns the same Some(r) for every value.
